item.title: Jaryd's News — Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Edmonton council heads to an Oct. 16 special meeting on the province’s infill rollback order; Watchdog: man who died in Edmonton police custody lay down in a release cell without biometric monitoring; Supreme Court of Canada splits 5–4 to uphold a three-year sentence in an Indigenous intimate-partner violence case; FBI arrests a Canadian citizen it calls a key suspect in the ShinyHunters breach of its jobs website; Magnitude 7.7 earthquake collapses buildings and roads in central Panama; at least 27 hurt, no deaths reported; Isaias makes landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane; hundreds of thousands lose power; Russian glide bombs kill at least 17 in Zaporizhzhia, a day after Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow; BCE, Rogers and Telus shares slide as SpaceX buys low-band spectrum for Starlink Mobile; Canada’s Weston family agrees to buy U.K. pharmacy chain Boots for US$8.9 billion. Plus Viral on social, Science corner, AI news and advances, Markets and the next Oilers game.

item.title: Edmonton council heads to an Oct. 16 special meeting on the province’s infill rollback order
item.description: A day after Premier Danielle Smith ordered Edmonton to return its zoning rules on housing types, density and building heights to their earlier form and restore pre-2020 minimum on-site parking, the city and province remained at odds Friday. Council has three months to comply and has scheduled a special meeting for Oct. 16 to discuss the directive and possible next steps, Global News reported. The province says the rules will stay in place while Edmonton spends 18 months on a broader land-use review with public consultation. Smith said the change addresses “unintended pressures on utilities, water supply, parking, [and] other municipal services.” Mayor Andrew Knack has said it will raise taxes and housing costs, and Alberta Municipalities called it provincial overreach. University of Alberta housing researcher Damian Collins told CTV News the city’s goal of putting half of new housing in established neighbourhoods depends heavily on infill, and that without it more growth would land on the city’s edges. The group Edmonton Neighbourhoods United welcomed the order as a chance for “meaningful community engagement.” Projects already approved or under construction aren’t clearly addressed in the reporting so far, and what the city can still change before the three-month deadline is one of the questions for the Oct. 16 meeting. Claims on both sides about effects on taxes, sprawl or parking are predictions, not measured results. Why it matters: The rules decide what can be built on many Edmonton residential lots, including how dense new homes can be and how much parking new projects must include.

item.title: Watchdog: man who died in Edmonton police custody lay down in a release cell without biometric monitoring
item.description: The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) released new details Friday on the Sept. 17 death of a 27-year-old man held at the Edmonton Police Service’s Detainee Management Unit. He was arrested Sept. 16 for alleged shoplifting and breaching release conditions, screened by an on-site paramedic and placed in a cell with biometric monitoring. After a justice of the peace ordered his release by video the next day, staff moved him just after 5:20 p.m. into a release cell with two other detainees while paperwork was finalized. That cell had cameras but no biometric monitoring. Video shows him moving until about 6:40 p.m., when he lay down on the floor; an officer found him unconscious at 7:02 p.m. He died before he could be taken to hospital. ASIRT says its investigation is at an early stage, and no cause of death has been released. The man hasn’t been named. ASIRT is part of the Police Review Commission, a civilian-led agency independent of police. Why it matters: It raises questions about how detainees are monitored in Edmonton’s holding cells in the final hours before release.

item.title: Supreme Court of Canada splits 5–4 to uphold a three-year sentence in an Indigenous intimate-partner violence case
item.description: In R. v. Cope, released Friday, the majority dismissed the Crown’s appeal and let stand the reduced three-year sentence of Harry Arthur Cope, a Mi’kmaw man with severe mental-health challenges who pleaded guilty in 2022 to aggravated assault against his partner, a Mi’kmaw woman. He had originally been sentenced to five years. The court set out a three-step approach: sentencing judges must consider the Criminal Code provisions on the over-incarceration of Indigenous people (the Gladue principles) together with newer provisions recognizing Indigenous women’s heightened vulnerability to violence, rather than treating them as competing. The majority said denunciation and deterrence don’t automatically require a longer prison term. The four dissenting judges said the result fails to reflect Parliament’s direction toward tougher sentences for such abuse, The Globe and Mail reported. The decision doesn’t create lighter sentences across the board: it says the two sets of provisions must be weighed together on the facts of each case, and a sentence can still be long where the circumstances call for it. Why it matters: The ruling now guides how judges across Canada, sentence intimate-partner violence cases involving Indigenous offenders and victims.

item.title: FBI arrests a Canadian citizen it calls a key suspect in the ShinyHunters breach of its jobs website
item.description: FBI Director Kash Patel said Friday that agents had arrested “another suspected co-conspirator” of the ShinyHunters group, which the bureau believes is behind last month’s breach of FBIjobs.gov, a platform run by a third-party vendor. The New York Times reported the suspect is a Canadian citizen arrested in Pennsylvania and considered a primary co-conspirator, according to BleepingComputer. The hackers claimed to have stolen 2 to 3 terabytes of data. Samples shared with media outlets confirmed exposed information on current and former FBI employees, including home addresses, Social Security numbers, sensitive job assignments and family members’ details, according to BleepingComputer. Patel said it was the latest of several arrests “in a matter of days” involving the network. The suspect hasn’t been officially named, and no charges had been made public at edition time. Names circulating on social media and YouTube haven’t been confirmed by the FBI or by reputable outlets. The size of the stolen data is the hackers’ own claim. Why it matters: A Canadian accused in a major U.S. federal breach could face extradition questions and shows how far ShinyHunters, also blamed for corporate data thefts, reaches.

item.title: Magnitude 7.7 earthquake collapses buildings and roads in central Panama; at least 27 hurt, no deaths reported
item.description: The quake struck at 12:56 p.m. local time Friday (11:56 a.m. MDT), centred about 10 km from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in Herrera province, the U.S. Geological Survey said. The USGS first estimated magnitude 8.0, then revised it to 7.6 and 7.7. A magnitude 6.6 quake followed that afternoon, among dozens of aftershocks. A tsunami warning for the eastern Pacific was issued and later lifted. Panama’s National Civil Protection System reported 27 people with minor injuries and no deaths, AFP reported. President José Raúl Mulino said “we are facing a major disaster,” with some roads “completely collapsed,” and went to Penonomé in Coclé province, where the bell tower of a 16th-century cathedral fell. Health Minister Fernando Boyd said Herrera, Coclé and Los Santos were hardest hit. The Panama Canal Authority said shipping was operating normally. Injury counts were early and may rise as remote areas are reached. Some quake clips circulating online are from other countries’ earlier earthquakes, so check the source before sharing. Canadians in Panama can register with Global Affairs Canada’s Registration of Canadians Abroad service. Why it matters: Panama is a popular destination for Canadian travellers and retirees, and the canal carries a significant share of Asia–North America trade.

item.title: Isaias makes landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane; hundreds of thousands lose power
item.description: The U.S. National Hurricane Center said Isaias came ashore near Destin on the Florida Panhandle at 8:30 p.m. CDT Friday (7:30 p.m. MDT) with sustained winds of 165 km/h after weakening from Category 3 before landfall. A gauge at Panama City Beach recorded water about 1.7 metres (5.6 feet) above normal high tide, and a gust of 187 km/h was measured near Santa Rosa Sound. The storm weakened quickly as it moved north through Alabama and was declared post-tropical by early Saturday. Hundreds of thousands of people in Alabama and the Panhandle were without power, The Associated Press reported; FOX Weather put outages above 750,000 at the peak. Heavy rain and flash-flood risk continue across the U.S. Southeast through the weekend. “Post-tropical” doesn’t mean harmless: the NHC says flooding rain and storm surge remained threats after landfall. No death toll had been confirmed by authorities at edition time. Why it matters: Many Canadian snowbirds own or rent along the Gulf Coast, and flights and travel through the region are disrupted this weekend.

item.title: Russian glide bombs kill at least 17 in Zaporizhzhia, a day after Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow
item.description: Russian forces dropped guided aerial bombs on residential areas of the southeastern Ukrainian city at about 4:48 a.m. local time Saturday, Ukrinform reported. Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the regional military administration, said the death toll had risen to 17, including three children, Kyiv Post reported; 26 residential buildings were damaged, including a direct hit on a five-storey apartment block. Sunday has been declared a day of mourning. President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote that Russia “expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports” with the strike. In a Friday call with Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin said an immediate resumption of three-way peace talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks during Russia’s elections last month, Al Jazeera reported, even as U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff called Friday’s Miami meeting with Ukrainian, European and NATO officials “constructive.” The death toll rose through Saturday morning, from 8 to 11 to 12 to 17 as reported by different outlets at different times; 17 was the latest official figure at edition time and may change. Russia says it targets military sites; independent verification inside the city comes mainly from reporters on scene, including AFP. Why it matters: Canada is one of Ukraine’s largest backers; the strike and Putin’s comments undercut hopes that U.S. concessions on Russian fuel would ease the war before winter.

item.title: BCE, Rogers and Telus shares slide as SpaceX buys low-band spectrum for Starlink Mobile
item.description: SpaceX agreed Thursday to buy Grain Management’s nationwide U.S. 800 MHz spectrum, up to 14 MHz of low-band airwaves that travel long distances and through buildings, for a planned Starlink Mobile network that would mix satellites and ground towers. The price wasn’t disclosed and the deal needs U.S. Federal Communications Commission approval. It adds to 65 MHz of mid-band spectrum SpaceX is buying from EchoStar, Ars Technica reported. Telecom stocks fell Friday on fears of satellite competition. T-Mobile slid 9.1 per cent and AT&T 7.4 per cent, and the TSX telecom index was down 4.5 per cent at one point, with BCE down nearly 5 per cent at midday, Reuters reported. Rogers closed down 3.7 per cent at $42.46, according to MarketWatch data. The licences are American; the deal doesn’t give SpaceX any Canadian spectrum, and the Canadian selloff was driven by investor sentiment. Starlink Mobile’s land-based network doesn’t exist yet. Not investment advice. Why it matters: Canadian carriers’ share prices matter to many pension and retirement portfolios, and more satellite-to-phone competition could eventually affect what Canadians pay for wireless.

item.title: Canada’s Weston family agrees to buy U.K. pharmacy chain Boots for US$8.9 billion
item.description: Wittington Investments, the Toronto-based holding company of the Weston family (which controls Loblaw), said this week it has a definitive agreement to buy Boots’ retail operations in the U.K. and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. The US$8.9-billion price includes assumed debt. The seller is The Boots Group, majority-owned by U.S. private-equity firm Sycamore Partners with Stefano Pessina’s family. Fairfax Financial will invest up to US$2.3 billion for a 50 per cent stake, with Wittington keeping operational control, the companies said. The deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. Wittington is the Westons’ private holding company, not Loblaw itself, so Loblaw shareholders aren’t directly buying Boots. Farmacias Benavides and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland stay with the sellers. Why it matters: It puts the family that controls Loblaw, owner of Shoppers Drug Mart, in charge of one of Britain’s best-known pharmacy chains.

item.title: Yes, the video of a Panama cathedral losing its bell tower in the earthquake is real
item.description: Widely shared footage shows the bell tower of the cathedral of San Juan Bautista in Penonomé, in Panama’s Coclé province, broken away and lying in rubble after Friday’s magnitude 7.7 earthquake. Other clips from Penonomé show part of a hotel collapsing onto parked cars. Verdict: Confirmed. The Associated Press published video of the 16th-century cathedral’s fallen tower, and Mexican and Dominican outlets showed the same scene and the hotel collapse. AFP reported that President José Raúl Mulino travelled to Penonomé to coordinate the response. A separate viral clip of water pouring off a Panama City skyscraper’s rooftop pool was reported by AFP but not independently verified, and some “Panama” compilations include footage from earlier quakes elsewhere. Why it matters: It’s some of the clearest verified footage of the quake’s damage, which was worst in central Panama.

item.title: Storm-surge videos from Destin and Fort Walton Beach as Isaias came ashore are real
item.description: Clips shared overnight show seawater pouring over roads and waterfront in Destin and Fort Walton Beach, Fla., and big waves at M.B. Miller Pier in Panama City Beach as Hurricane Isaias made landfall. Verdict: Confirmed. Local stations WJHG and Atlanta News First and FOX Weather published the footage, and the National Hurricane Center reported water about 1.7 metres above normal high tide at Panama City Beach. Old hurricane videos from earlier storms often get recycled during new ones; these clips were posted by the stations that filmed them during Isaias. Why it matters: It shows why officials ordered evacuations: storm surge, not wind, is usually a hurricane’s deadliest hazard.

item.title: Claim: a video shows a woman rescuing a white baby reindeer
item.description: A heart-warming clip of a woman freeing and cuddling a rare white reindeer calf is spreading as a real rescue. Verdict: False. It’s AI-generated. Lead Stories found the original Instagram account labelled it “AI Content,” Meta also flagged it as AI, and the video has tell-tale glitches, such as antlers passing through the woman’s body and objects appearing and disappearing. This verdict rests on one fact-checker’s review plus the original poster’s own “AI Content” label. Look for that label, and for body parts or objects that merge or vanish, before sharing animal-rescue videos. Why it matters: Feel-good animal-rescue clips are one of the most common kinds of AI fakes this fall.

item.title: “DNA Typewriter” records the family tree of 1.3 million cells in a developing mouse
item.description: In a paper published in Science this week, a team led by Jay Shendure of the University of Washington and Chengxiang Qiu of Dartmouth College inserted a molecular recorder, called DNA Typewriter, into the genome of a fertilized mouse egg. Each time a cell divides, the recorder uses gene editing to “type” a new mark onto a stretch of DNA, in order and without overwriting earlier marks, so every descendant cell carries a log of its ancestry. Reading those logs out of about 1.3 million cells, the team reconstructed the cells’ family tree from the first division of the egg to day 13.5 of development, when organs are forming. A redesigned “tape” made the records easier to read from individual cells, the university said. This was done in a single mouse embryo in the lab; it’s a research tool, not a medical treatment. The findings have been described by the team and the university; independent researchers will need to reproduce them. Why it matters: Tracing which early cells give rise to which tissues could help researchers understand birth defects, developmental disorders and cancer.

item.title: Three fired OpenAI safety researchers say they were pushed out for prioritizing safety; OpenAI says they mishandled sensitive data
item.description: Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, dismissed by OpenAI last week, published an open letter Thursday to the company’s Safety and Security Committee and advisory groups denying they broke company policy. They warned their firing has made former colleagues “afraid to speak” and could weaken work with outside safety evaluators. “I believe we were fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation,” Balesni wrote on X. Korbak said he had raised concerns that OpenAI was “losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think.” OpenAI has repeatedly denied the allegations, saying the three were fired for “accessing and handling sensitive company information” outside established procedures, reportedly involving sharing with a third-party AI safety organization, and that it hasn’t abandoned its safety commitments. This is a dispute between the two sides’ accounts; neither has released the documents at issue, and no regulator or court has ruled on it. Why it matters: OpenAI’s models are used by Canadian governments and businesses, and outside testing by independent safety groups is one of the few checks on how they behave.

item.title: Jaryd's News — Friday, Oct. 9, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta Court of Appeal rules 4–1 that Ottawa’s amended Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional; Two teens wounded in a drive-by shooting near Saddleback Road in south Edmonton; a youth is charged; Poilievre urges Ottawa to sue Stelco’s U.S. owner as Hamilton layoffs begin; Carney answers Musk’s separation posts: Canada’s future “will be decided by Canadians”; U.S. sanctions the International Criminal Court itself; Canada joins allies in “strongly” disagreeing; Trump says Putin agreed to send Russian diesel to world markets; Zelensky calls it a “gift to Putin”; Saudi-led coalition launches a large-scale offensive against Yemen’s Houthis, claiming 136 targets destroyed; Isaias hits Category 3 and is set to make landfall on the western Florida Panhandle this evening; TSX jumps 519 points, its biggest gain in five weeks, as weak jobs data cool rate-hike bets; Aritzia shares soar about 20% after a 44% revenue jump and a raised outlook. Plus Viral on social, Science corner, AI news and advances, Markets and the next Oilers game.

item.title: Alberta Court of Appeal rules 4–1 that Ottawa’s amended Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional
item.description: In an opinion released Friday, Reference re Impact Assessment Act, as amended (2026 ABCA 320), four of five Alberta Court of Appeal justices found that the federal law’s “designated projects” regime still reaches into provincial jurisdiction, even after Parliament amended it in 2024 following the Supreme Court of Canada’s 2023 ruling against much of the original act. Justice Kevin Feehan dissented. Alberta brought the reference, with Ontario and Saskatchewan backing it, The Canadian Press reported. The majority said the act still lets Ottawa stop or set conditions on a project within provincial jurisdiction if it has even a narrow federal effect. “The (Impact Assessment Act) creates great uncertainty due to the potential for previously unpronounced standards to apply to designated projects,” the court wrote. It found that part of the law and its project-list regulations unconstitutional except where they apply to federal undertakings, according to the Canadian Constitution Foundation, an intervener. A reference opinion is advisory: it doesn’t by itself strike the law off the books, and Ottawa can appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada as of right, as it did after the court’s 2022 opinion. At edition time, Canadian Press was the only news organization outside excluded outlets reporting the ruling; this summary is checked against the court’s own opinion and the intervener’s statement. This edition didn’t find a federal response yet. Why it matters: The act governs federal reviews of big Alberta projects such as mines and pipelines; former premier Jason Kenney dubbed it the “no more pipelines act.”

item.title: Two teens wounded in a drive-by shooting near Saddleback Road in south Edmonton; a youth is charged
item.description: Edmonton police say a 15-year-old and a 16-year-old were taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries after shots were fired from a vehicle in a shopping-centre parking lot near Saddleback Road and 27 Avenue at about 1:20 p.m. CTV News reports it happened Thursday afternoon. The vehicle drove off, but a male youth has since been charged; police said the accused and the victims know each other. Nearby Sweet Grass School was briefly placed on lockdown, CityNews reported. Reports differ on small details: one outlet’s copy lists a 10:20 p.m. time and “southwest” in its headline, which conflict with the 1:20 p.m. time and southeast location in the other reports. Because the accused is a youth, their name can’t be published under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, and the charges haven’t been tested in court. Why it matters: It happened in the middle of the afternoon at a busy south-side shopping area next to a school.

item.title: Poilievre urges Ottawa to sue Stelco’s U.S. owner as Hamilton layoffs begin
item.description: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre on Friday called on the federal government to sue Cleveland-Cliffs, the Ohio-based owner of Stelco, as soon as Monday, seeking to bring back workers and restart production or force a sale to a Canadian owner. Speaking in Burlington, Ont., across the harbour from Stelco’s Hamilton works, he also proposed scrapping the industrial carbon tax, cracking down on Chinese steel imports, speeding up LNG projects and negotiating a tariff-free deal with the U.S. Stelco says up to 500 workers at its Hamilton and Lake Erie sites could be laid off; the first layoffs take effect Sunday, with about 330 Hamilton workers affected over three weeks, according to United Steelworkers Local 1005. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly gave Cleveland-Cliffs five business days on Monday to show how it will meet its employment commitments or face legal action. CEO Lourenco Goncalves said the layoffs are temporary and workers would be recalled if Canada and the U.S. reach a steel trade deal. Whether Ottawa can win such a suit depends on the confidential undertakings Cleveland-Cliffs gave when it bought Stelco, which haven’t been made public. The Conservative plan is an opposition proposal, not government policy. Why it matters: It’s a test of whether Ottawa will enforce the job promises foreign buyers make under the Investment Canada Act, with steel tariffs still weighing on Canadian producers.

item.title: Carney answers Musk’s separation posts: Canada’s future “will be decided by Canadians”
item.description: Asked on Thursday in Sherbrooke, Que., about Elon Musk’s posts saying Quebec should separate and Alberta and Saskatchewan should follow, Prime Minister Mark Carney said: “The future of Canada will be decided by Canadians and the priorities of Canadians, the priorities of the people of Quebec.” He said Canadians should be free from interference by foreign governments “and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do.” Posts on X don’t change the legal path: the Oct. 19 Alberta vote won’t separate the province on its own, and under the federal Clarity Act the House of Commons must judge whether any secession question is clear and whether a clear majority supported it before negotiations could begin. Why it matters: Albertans vote Oct. 19 on a non-binding question asking whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the constitutional process toward a binding separation referendum.

item.title: U.S. sanctions the International Criminal Court itself; Canada joins allies in “strongly” disagreeing
item.description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sanctions on the ICC as an institution on Friday, banning U.S. entities from transactions with what he called a “rogue court.” “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” he said. Exemptions create what amounts to a six-month grace period, which the State Department said gives member states time to address U.S. objections. The court called the move “an assault on the rule of law” and said “history will judge this moment.” Canada joined the U.K., France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Denmark and the Netherlands in a joint statement saying they “regret and strongly disagree with” the sanctions. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called it “a serious blow,” while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces an ICC arrest warrant, praised it. The announcement came hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize. Neither the U.S. nor Israel is a member of the ICC, and both reject its jurisdiction over their citizens. The U.S. objections centre on the court’s past Afghanistan inquiry involving U.S. personnel and its warrant for Netanyahu. The grace period can be shortened or extended depending on talks, the State Department said, so the full financial effect isn’t yet known. Why it matters: Canada is a founding supporter of the ICC; the sanctions could cut the court off from U.S. banks and software it relies on, and put Ottawa at odds with Washington.

item.title: Trump says Putin agreed to send Russian diesel to world markets; Zelensky calls it a “gift to Putin”
item.description: After a phone call with Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump said Friday that Russia will “immediately” supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to U.S. and global markets, another 500,000 tonnes in November and a million tonnes after that. The U.S. Treasury said it is issuing a temporary general licence allowing Russian diesel onto the global market, a waiver on some sanctions. The Kremlin said the leaders also discussed ending the war. Volodymyr Zelensky wrote that “gifts to Putin will not bring peace” and called sanctions relief without a de-escalation deal “an obvious weakness.” The announcement came as Ukrainian, European, U.S. and NATO officials met in Miami; envoy Steve Witkoff called the talks constructive and said participants agreed to keep working toward ending the war. The volumes are Trump’s figures and haven’t been confirmed by Russia in detail. An Atlantic Council analyst told Axios the amounts are “uncertain to materialize” and small next to a global shortfall of millions of barrels a day of refining capacity. No ceasefire or deal was announced in Miami. Why it matters: Diesel prices are near record highs amid the Iran war; any easing affects trucking, farming and fuel costs in Canada, while the sanctions waiver eases pressure on Russia.

item.title: Saudi-led coalition launches a large-scale offensive against Yemen’s Houthis, claiming 136 targets destroyed
item.description: Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said Friday night that the coalition is conducting a large-scale operation against Houthi fighters and military capabilities, including efforts to dismantle the group’s ballistic-missile network, and that it had destroyed 136 military targets. It says it is giving round-the-clock air support to Yemeni government forces, whose offensive aims to retake Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa. The target count and the Yemeni government’s claim of more than 1,400 Houthi fighters “neutralized” are combatants’ own figures and can’t be independently verified. Arab News is Saudi-owned. Casualty figures from inside Houthi-held areas weren’t available. Why it matters: A wider Yemen war threatens Red Sea and Gulf shipping already disrupted by the Iran conflict, keeping pressure on global oil and fuel prices.

item.title: Isaias hits Category 3 and is set to make landfall on the western Florida Panhandle this evening
item.description: At 3 p.m. MDT the U.S. National Hurricane Center put Isaias about 145 km south of Pensacola with sustained winds of 185 km/h, a Category 3 major hurricane, moving north at 28 km/h. It expects landfall on the western Florida Panhandle this evening, then a track across Alabama into the Tennessee Valley. The NHC warns of storm surge of up to 6 to 9 feet (about 2 to 3 metres) from the Alabama–Florida line to Grayton Beach, hurricane-force winds up to 160 km inland, and 4 to 8 inches (100 to 200 mm) of rain. Escambia County, which includes Pensacola, ordered evacuations of low-lying zones including Pensacola Beach and Perdido Key, the Pensacola News Journal reported, and ABC News reported evacuation orders in Florida and Alabama counties. Hurricane categories measure wind only; surge and inland flooding usually cause the most deaths. Forecasts can shift by tens of kilometres, so landfall location and timing may differ from the advisory. Why it matters: The Gulf Coast is a popular route for Canadian snowbirds and travellers this time of year; anyone there should follow local evacuation orders.

item.title: TSX jumps 519 points, its biggest gain in five weeks, as weak jobs data cool rate-hike bets
item.description: The S&P/TSX composite index closed Friday at 35,664.62, up 519.24 points or 1.48 per cent, its biggest one-day gain since Sept. 3 and highest close in two weeks, Reuters reported. Investors read Friday’s loss of 68,000 jobs as reducing the chance of a Bank of Canada rate hike. Materials rose 2.81 per cent as gold climbed, and energy rose 1.07 per cent. The index ended the week up 0.46 per cent after two weekly declines. In New York, the Dow rose 423.31 points to 51,654.95, the S&P 500 rose 46.18 to 7,811.54 and the Nasdaq rose 172.83 to 27,366.17. November crude settled up 36 cents at US$91.85 a barrel, December gold rose US$59.30 to US$4,216.30, and the loonie was at 70.07 U.S. cents, down from 70.22, according to The Canadian Press. The Bank of Canada’s next decision is Oct. 28; market pricing of rate odds is a forecast, not a decision. One-day moves say little about longer trends. Not investment advice. Why it matters: Lower odds of a rate hike matter for Alberta mortgage holders and borrowers; energy stocks gained with oil holding above US$90.

item.title: Aritzia shares soar about 20% after a 44% revenue jump and a raised outlook
item.description: Vancouver-based clothing retailer Aritzia reported Thursday that second-quarter revenue rose 44 per cent to $1.17 billion, with U.S. revenue up 60 per cent to $779 million. Adjusted earnings were $1.31 a share, up from 59 cents a year earlier and above analysts’ forecasts of $1.05, the Financial Post reported. It raised its full-year revenue outlook to $4.78 billion to $4.88 billion and plans six new U.S. boutiques this quarter. Its Toronto-listed shares closed Friday at $146.91, up about 20.5 per cent from Thursday’s close of $121.89, according to Yahoo Finance data, and helped lead the TSX higher. Part of the quarter’s profit came from one-time tariff refunds, which won’t recur; the adjusted figures are the company’s own measure. Not investment advice. Why it matters: It’s a rare Canadian retailer growing quickly in the U.S. despite the trade fight; it also booked about $97 million in refunds of U.S. tariffs a court ruled illegal.

item.title: Videos of two house explosions in Hamilton, Ont., are real; three people were hurt
item.description: Footage widely shared since Thursday shows a debris field and fire after a garage exploded on Springside Drive on Hamilton Mountain at about 7:30 a.m., and a second blast about 90 minutes later on Lampton Place in the east end that partly collapsed a home. One person was burned in the first blast; neighbours pulled two elderly residents from the second house, Fire Chief Dave Cunliffe said. Verdict: Confirmed. The explosions were 17 km apart and the fire chief says they aren’t related. The Ontario Fire Marshal is investigating; neighbours reported smelling natural gas before the Lampton Place blast, which is the main focus there. No cause has been confirmed for either explosion, and officials haven’t found any link between the two. Why it matters: It’s a reminder that a natural-gas smell means leave the building and call 911 or your gas utility from outside.

item.title: Yes, a Florida college student really built a chair bridge to help a stranger across floodwater
item.description: A TikTok clip with more than 50 million views shows a Flagler College student in St. Augustine, Fla., moving chairs one by one through a flooded walkway so a woman can step across without getting wet. Both people in the video identified themselves in the comments. Verdict: Confirmed. The St. Johns Citizen identified the original poster and reported that both students confirmed in the comments that it was them. Many commenters assume the pair are a couple; there’s no evidence of that. The original video is on TikTok; no reputable news channel had posted it on YouTube, so no clip is embedded here. Why it matters: A feel-good clip that is what it appears to be.

item.title: The video of a guest diving off an Epcot boat ride is real, and Disney has banned the group
item.description: A clip shows a man climbing out of a boat on Epcot’s Gran Fiesta Tour ride at Walt Disney World and diving headfirst into the shallow water. The ride was reportedly stopped for about 15 minutes. Verdict: Confirmed. Disney said the guest and his party broke park rules and were trespassed from the property, Entertainment Weekly and People reported. Disney hasn’t said whether the man was hurt or identified him. No reputable news channel had posted the clip on YouTube, so none is embedded. Why it matters: Ride channels are often only knee-deep; diving in is dangerous and gets you banned.

item.title: Claim: viral videos show the Houthi strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid Airport
item.description: Clips of burning aircraft and smoke over a runway are circulating as footage of this week’s Houthi missile attack on Riyadh’s main airport. Verdict: False. Fact-checkers found the most-shared clips are recycled or fake: one is 2017 footage of a ground-equipment fire at Jeddah airport, another is AI-generated, and others show unrelated fires, including an earlier Riyadh neighbourhood fire and a Russian drone attack. Authorities confirmed three deaths in the attacks on the Riyadh and Abha airports. Reverse image search is the quickest check for recycled war videos. Why it matters: The attack itself was real (three Saudis were killed), but the most dramatic “footage” isn’t from it.

item.title: Cornell team makes a working transistor from a 7-electronvolt semiconductor, the widest bandgap yet
item.description: Writing in Nature this week, a Cornell-led team reports silicon-doped aluminium gallium oxide films, α-(AlGa)₂O₃, with bandgaps above 7.0 electronvolts, wider than cubic boron nitride, previously the widest-bandgap semiconductor known. Materials with gaps this large normally behave as insulators, but the team grew the films on sapphire with a technique called suboxide molecular-beam epitaxy and got room-temperature conductivity more than 100 million times higher than earlier attempts in this range. They built working devices from it: a Schottky diode and a field-effect transistor they call the AlphaFET. In an accompanying commentary, Hironori Okumura of Japan’s University of Tsukuba said the work “pushes semiconductors into a regime that has long been reserved for insulators.” These are lab demonstrations, not products; device performance, reliability and manufacturing at scale still have to be shown. Silicon carbide and gallium nitride remain the commercial wide-bandgap materials today. Why it matters: Wider bandgaps let power electronics handle higher voltages more efficiently in less space, which matters for grids, EV chargers and data centres.

item.title: Anthropic launches free AI vulnerability scans for open-source projects and a program to defend power and water systems
item.description: Anthropic announced an “Anthropic Cyber Mission” with two parts. A Critical Infrastructure Defense Program brings its Claude models and on-site engineers to security firms that protect grids, water systems and plants; 11 founding partners include CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Dragos, Accenture, Deloitte, Hitachi and Rockwell Automation. A free OSS Scanner gives eligible open-source projects periodic vulnerability scans with reproducible reports and suggested fixes. Anthropic says its models flagged more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities in widely used software over six months. In an accuracy check, expert testers cleared 85 of 97 critical and high-severity findings for disclosure, SiliconANGLE reported. The company also pledged $150 million over three years to the U.S. government’s Genesis Mission science program. Effectiveness figures are Anthropic’s own. Axios noted Anthropic hasn’t disclosed commercial terms for partners or who covers computing costs, and Anthropic says unreviewed scanner reports may contain errors such as wrong severity ratings. Why it matters: Operators of utilities, including in Alberta, run decades-old equipment that’s hard to patch; AI tools are being aimed at both finding and fixing those weaknesses.

item.title: Jaryd's News — Friday, Oct. 9, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Province orders Edmonton to scrap its 2024 infill zoning rules within three months and bring back parking minimums; Cold Lake First Nations asks the Federal Court to quash Pacific Link’s “national interest” designation; Snowfall warning for west-central Alberta; Edmonton’s rain turns to wet snow tonight, about 2 cm Saturday; Ottawa announces $2-billion heat-pump rebate: up to $10,000 for households below median income; Major-projects bill C-39 passes its first House vote 296–26 with Conservative support; Former UN rights chief Navi Pillay wins the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize; Trump says the U.S. won’t attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms; the naval blockade stays; Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh’s main airport kill three Saudis, including a Saudia pilot; Ukrainian and European officials meet U.S. envoys in Miami on a “new, unified” plan to end the war; Hurricane Isaias nears major-hurricane strength with landfall on the Alabama–Florida coast expected tonight; Canada sheds 68,000 jobs in September and unemployment rises to 6.5%, but Alberta adds 23,000; Oil slips after Trump rules out pre-midterm Iran strikes; TSX ended Thursday up 0.3%. Plus Viral on social, Science corner, AI news and advances, Markets and the next Oilers game.

item.title: Province orders Edmonton to scrap its 2024 infill zoning rules within three months and bring back parking minimums
item.description: Premier Danielle Smith and Municipal Affairs Minister Dan Williams announced Thursday that Edmonton must, within three months, revert its residential infill rules on housing types, density and height to those in place before the city’s January 2024 zoning overhaul, and restore the minimum on-site parking requirements that applied before 2020. The city then has 18 months to review its land-use bylaw. Calgary, which already repealed blanket rezoning, was told to keep that repeal while its own review finishes next year. Williams said the order will be formalized by cabinet order in council and called it “a reset,” adding: “It’s not an ultimatum, but a conversation.” Smith said communities had been “blindsided” and that “when municipalities have taken actions that are undermining people’s property value, then we have to step in.” Mayor Andrew Knack said the city was told the day before, warned of higher property taxes and housing costs, and said he will likely call an emergency council meeting next week. Alberta Municipalities president Dylan Bressey called it an “expensive attack on municipal autonomy,” while Coun. Karen Principe and the group Edmonton Neighbourhoods United backed the move. Alberta’s Municipal Government Act lets the province direct a municipality to change its bylaws, so this is within provincial power; the dispute is over whether it should be used here. Claims about effects on property values, taxes and affordability come from each side and haven’t been independently measured yet; city administration has a report on infill’s effect on neighbouring property values due by the third quarter of 2027. Why it matters: It decides what can be built on residential lots across Edmonton, including the eight-unit multiplexes that have been approved automatically under the 2024 rules, and touches property values, rents and taxes.

item.title: Cold Lake First Nations asks the Federal Court to quash Pacific Link’s “national interest” designation
item.description: Cold Lake First Nations filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court on Thursday challenging Ottawa’s Oct. 1 decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline, which would carry up to one million barrels of oil a day from Alberta to the B.C. coast, as a project in the national interest under the Building Canada Act. It asks the court to quash the designation and declare that Canada owes the Nation a duty to consult. The application says the decision breached Canadian law and is inconsistent with the honour of the Crown, and that “increasing oilsands production will have significant adverse effects” on members’ Treaty 6 way of life. The Nation says it supports responsible development and wants meaningful consultation on both Pacific Link and the linked Pathways carbon-capture project, whose storage hub would sit in its traditional territory. Filing for judicial review doesn’t stop the project; a court would first have to hear the case. The Nation says the legal action “does not close the door” to working with Ottawa. Prime Minister Carney has said Indigenous communities would be offered at least 10 per cent ownership, but that offer isn’t the same thing as the consultation the Nation says it was denied. Why it matters: Pacific Link is the centrepiece of the Canada–Alberta energy deal; a court fight could affect the plan to finish reviews within a year and start construction next September.

item.title: Snowfall warning for west-central Alberta; Edmonton’s rain turns to wet snow tonight, about 2 cm Saturday
item.description: Environment Canada issued a yellow snowfall warning at 4:48 a.m. Friday for west-central Alberta, including Hinton and Grande Prairie, saying rain will turn to snow today and accumulating snow will become widespread by this evening. Totals will be “highly variable,” from about 7 to 25 cm: lower in valleys such as the Jasper and Grande Prairie townsites, higher on high ground such as Highway 40 between Grande Prairie and Hinton. “Travel will likely be challenging.” For Edmonton, a special weather statement remains in effect. The 5 a.m. forecast calls for a high of 11°C today, 5 to 10 mm of rain tonight changing to wet snow overnight, then snow Saturday with about 2 cm and a temperature steady near 1°C. Sunday is cloudy with a high of 4°C, and Thanksgiving Monday is sunny with a high of 9°C. Only light snow is expected in Calgary, though more significant amounts are possible against the southern foothills and south of Calgary, where snow continues Sunday. A special weather statement is a lower-level alert than a warning; only west-central Alberta is under a snowfall warning so far. Amounts on the Edmonton–Calgary corridor remain uncertain, so check Environment Canada and 511 Alberta before driving. Why it matters: It’s a long weekend with heavy highway travel; drivers heading west toward Hinton, Jasper or Grande Prairie face the worst of it.

item.title: Ottawa announces $2-billion heat-pump rebate: up to $10,000 for households below median income
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney announced in Sherbrooke, Que., on Thursday a $2-billion, eight-year program aimed at one million home retrofits. Households below the median income would get up to $10,000 toward a heat pump and other homeowners $2,000; the money also helps apartment owners retrofit 280,000 units. The government says applications will go through an online portal with approval within 24 hours and no required energy audits, and the program is expected to start early next year. “Heat pumps are cleaner and safer than oil and electric furnaces. They are two to three times more efficient,” Carney said. The Canadian Press reports the program targets people needing emergency or near-term replacement of a heating system, while the earlier oil-to-heat-pump program is being wound down. The CP report says program details haven’t been finalized. The emissions estimate (more than 25 million tonnes) and the “two to three times more efficient” claim are the government’s; heat-pump savings depend on climate, model and local gas versus electricity prices, and very cold days may need backup heat. Why it matters: Most Alberta homes heat with natural gas, and cold-climate performance matters; the full eligibility rules, including for Albertans, haven’t been published yet.

item.title: Major-projects bill C-39 passes its first House vote 296–26 with Conservative support
item.description: Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, passed second reading Thursday 296–26 and was sent to a special legislative committee. The Conservatives voted with the Liberals; the Bloc Québécois, NDP and Greens voted against. The omnibus bill aims to speed approvals for major projects and changes the Canada Labour Code, adding special mediators and a national-interest test for when the labour minister can intervene in a strike or lockout. NDP parliamentary leader Don Davies said “you cannot build a stronger Canada, at the expense of workers’ rights,” and the Canadian Labour Congress said the labour changes should be removed. Federally regulated employers, through FETCO, said the bill doesn’t go far enough because it doesn’t let the minister act before a work stoppage. The committee isn’t expected to meet until the House returns the week of Oct. 19. Second reading approves a bill in principle; it can still be amended at committee and must pass third reading and the Senate. The NDP, which lacks official party status, has no seat on the committee but can propose amendments. Why it matters: The bill is the legal machinery behind fast-tracking projects like Pacific Link, and its labour rules would apply to federally regulated workplaces in Alberta such as railways, airlines and ports.

item.title: Former UN rights chief Navi Pillay wins the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
item.description: The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the prize Friday to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, 85, “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.” Born in Durban under apartheid, she defended Nelson Mandela and other anti-apartheid activists, then served as a judge on South Africa’s High Court, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court, and as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. The committee says she now sits as a judge at the International Court of Justice in the case in which Myanmar is accused of genocide. The committee credited her with a key role when the Rwanda tribunal established that rape and sexual violence could constitute genocide and crimes against humanity. It received 287 nominations. Pillay joked in Nuremberg, “If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump,” adding, “Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this.” The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor and will be presented in Oslo on Dec. 10. Pillay also chaired the UN commission of inquiry that found last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza; Israel dismissed that report as “scandalous.” The Nobel citation focuses on her overall legal career, not that finding. Why it matters: It’s a pointed endorsement of international courts at a time when, as the committee put it, judges are being sanctioned and their institutions attacked; Canada is a founding supporter of the ICC.

item.title: Trump says the U.S. won’t attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms; the naval blockade stays
item.description: “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections,” President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social late Thursday, citing “productive discussions” with Tehran and saying “the Blockade will remain in full force and effect.” Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Tehran is reviewing the U.S. response to its seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and would answer within days. Axios reported that before the post, the Pentagon had told Central Command to finish preparations for resuming major combat, and that U.S. officials had briefed Israel’s military chief on the possibility of renewed strikes within three weeks. Iranian media reported explosions in the southern Strait of Hormuz on Friday, which Fars attributed to tankers on “unauthorised” routes possibly hitting mines. Axios notes Trump’s past statements about Iran haven’t always matched what he did: before the June 2025 strikes and again before the war began in February, he said he hadn’t decided when he already had. The Hormuz explosion reports come from Iranian state-linked media and hadn’t been independently confirmed. Why it matters: Oil dropped on the pledge (see Business), which feeds into Canadian gas prices and Alberta’s royalty revenue.

item.title: Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh’s main airport kill three Saudis, including a Saudia pilot
item.description: Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said two attacks Thursday on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh hit airport facilities and a Saudia aircraft, killing three Saudi citizens and injuring others. Saudia confirmed the death of Capt. Hamoud Ali Alkalthami. Yemen’s Houthis said they fired missiles at the airport. Operations had resumed by Friday. Saudi authorities said earlier attacks this week killed three people at the Riyadh and Abha airports. The Saudi-led coalition said it would “punish” the Houthis and reported destroying rocket launch platforms. The escalation follows a Houthi offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandeb strait and a government counter-offensive; the UN says more than 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since July. Houthi claims about which weapons were used and other targets hit, including Najran, haven’t been confirmed by Saudi authorities. RTÉ notes claims by the warring parties are hard to verify independently because access for journalists is limited. Why it matters: Global Affairs Canada advisories and airline schedules for the Gulf can change fast; Canadians travelling through Riyadh should check with their airline before flying.

item.title: Ukrainian and European officials meet U.S. envoys in Miami on a “new, unified” plan to end the war
item.description: A Ukrainian delegation led by Kyrylo Budanov, head of the president’s office, and including Foreign Intelligence Service chief Rustem Umerov is in Miami for two days of talks starting Friday with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. A senior U.S. official told NBC News the talks will centre on “a new, unified proposal that is focused on all aspects of the conflict.” National security advisers from France, Germany and the U.K., the European Commission and NATO are also taking part; Russia is not. Euronews reports the options include a targeted ceasefire covering the Black Sea, energy facilities, or both. “We see on the part of the United States of America, an intensification of talks and meetings,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week there “don’t seem to be prospects of a negotiated settlement” right now. The details of the “new” plan haven’t been published, and previous rounds since September produced no announced breakthrough. Casualty figures come from Ukrainian officials. Why it matters: Canada is part of the coalition planning security guarantees for Ukraine, so any partial ceasefire deal would shape what Canadian commitments look like.

item.title: Hurricane Isaias nears major-hurricane strength with landfall on the Alabama–Florida coast expected tonight
item.description: At 7 a.m. CDT (6 a.m. MDT) the U.S. National Hurricane Center put Isaias about 390 km south of Pensacola, Fla., with maximum sustained winds near 175 km/h, moving north-northeast at 24 km/h. It is “likely to become a major hurricane this morning” and to make landfall within the hurricane warning zone tonight or early Saturday; forecasters expect some weakening from wind shear but say it will remain dangerous, with high-end Category 2 their best estimate at landfall. A hurricane warning runs from Ocean Springs, Miss., to the Bay/Gulf County line in Florida, and a storm-surge warning from the mouth of the Mississippi to the Suwannee River, with surge of 1.5 to 2 metres possible. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered non-residents out of Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island, Escambia County, Fla., ordered evacuations of zones A and B, and Pensacola’s airport was closing to commercial flights Friday morning, AP reported. The NHC says “it would only take about a 6 (hour) delay in the onset of the shear to bring a stronger hurricane than expected onshore,” so landfall strength remains uncertain. Rely on NHC and local officials rather than model screenshots on social media. Why it matters: Canadians on Thanksgiving-weekend trips to the Gulf Coast or U.S. Southeast should follow local evacuation orders; heavy rain and gusty winds are forecast well inland through the weekend.

item.title: Canada sheds 68,000 jobs in September and unemployment rises to 6.5%, but Alberta adds 23,000
item.description: Statistics Canada said Friday that employment fell by 68,000 (−0.3 per cent) in September, a second straight monthly drop after August’s loss of 42,000, and the unemployment rate rose 0.1 points to 6.5 per cent. Economists polled by Reuters had expected a gain of about 9,200 jobs, The Globe and Mail reported before the release. The losses were concentrated among youth aged 15 to 24 (−48,000) and in educational services (−35,000), health care and social assistance (−23,000) and manufacturing (−13,000); public-sector employment fell for a fourth month. Alberta bucked the trend: employment rose by 23,000 (+0.9 per cent) and the province’s unemployment rate fell 0.4 points to 6.4 per cent; Alberta employment is up 76,000 from a year earlier. Quebec lost 49,000 jobs and B.C. 20,000. Average hourly wages rose 2.3 per cent from a year earlier, and the participation rate fell to 64.8 per cent, the lowest since December 1997 outside the pandemic, which the agency links largely to population aging. The Labour Force Survey is based on a sample of about 65,000 households, and Statistics Canada warns that monthly estimates “may show more sampling variability than trends observed over longer periods.” The figures reflect the reference week of Sept. 13 to 19, and the survey doesn’t say what caused the declines. The data came out at 6:30 a.m. MDT, minutes before this edition; the figures here are taken directly from Statistics Canada, and news coverage of the release wasn’t yet available to cross-check. Why it matters: Alberta’s labour market is outperforming the country, while the national weakness is the last jobs report the Bank of Canada sees before its Oct. 28 rate decision.

item.title: Oil slips after Trump rules out pre-midterm Iran strikes; TSX ended Thursday up 0.3%
item.description: Brent crude futures were at US$102.80 a barrel at 6:05 a.m. MDT Friday, down about 1.4 per cent from Thursday’s settlement of US$104.28, and U.S. crude at US$90.57, down about 1 per cent, according to Yahoo Finance data. The Wall Street Journal and others tied the drop to Trump’s pledge not to attack Iran before Nov. 3, though attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz limited the decline. On Thursday the S&P/TSX composite index closed at 35,145.38, up 103.52 points or 0.3 per cent, as energy stocks rose with oil. The loonie was near 70.3 U.S. cents early Friday. Futures prices move minute to minute; these are early-morning snapshots, not closing prices. Not investment advice. Why it matters: Oil around US$100 helps Alberta producers and provincial revenue but keeps fuel prices high; each swing in Iran headlines moves both.

item.title: Video of Taal Volcano blasting a dark ash plume and volcanic lightning near Manila is real
item.description: Footage shared widely since Thursday evening shows a dark-grey column rising from Taal Volcano, south of Manila. The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) said a minor phreatomagmatic eruption at the main crater lasted about five minutes, sent the plume about 4,000 metres high, and that its cameras caught volcanic lightning in the plume. Verdict: Confirmed. Phivolcs kept Alert Level 1 and warned of possible thin ashfall in Agoncillo, Lemery, San Nicolas, Taal and nearby areas, as reported by GMA News, the Philippine News Agency and Al Jazeera. Some reposts describe the plume as 4,000 feet; Phivolcs’ figure is 4,000 metres. Be wary of older Taal footage from the much larger 2020 eruption being recirculated as new. Why it matters: The clips are genuine, but this was a short, minor eruption; Alert Level 1 is the lowest level above normal.

item.title: Posts saying arrests and detentions of Canadians in the U.S. jumped about 60% are right, but the number is 577
item.description: Global Affairs Canada’s annual consular data report, released Thursday, recorded 577 arrest and detention cases involving Canadians in the U.S. between April 2025 and March 2026, up nearly 60 per cent from 361 the year before. Over the same period Canadian visits to the U.S. fell to about 20.2 million, Statistics Canada data in the report show. Verdict: Confirmed, with a correction: some posts and early reports cite 557 cases; the report says 577. Worldwide, Ottawa opened 1,981 arrest and detention cases, about 20 per cent more than the previous year. The report doesn’t explain the increase. Linking it to U.S. immigration enforcement is a reasonable reading, but it comes from immigration lawyers and commentators, not from Global Affairs. Many cases involve Canadians living in the U.S., not just visitors. Why it matters: If you travel to or live in the U.S., Ottawa urges registering with its Registration of Canadians Abroad service and checking travel advice first.

item.title: Yes, Instagram really was suggesting Creed’s “Higher” for everyone’s Stories, and it has admitted the glitch
item.description: Users have joked for weeks that Instagram kept proposing Creed’s 1999 hit “Higher” as the soundtrack for unrelated Stories, with some suspecting a paid promotion. An Instagram spokesperson said the company “looked into this and found that this song is being recommended to more people than intended,” that it doesn’t yet know why, and that engineers are working on a fix. Verdict: Confirmed. Instagram added that the surge in suggestions for Soulja Boy’s “Turn My Swag On” is not a glitch and reflects how popular the song is on the platform. Instagram hasn’t said how many users were affected or when the fix will land. The “Creed paid Meta” theory has no evidence behind it. Why it matters: It’s a real algorithm bug, not a secret deal; there’s no evidence the band paid for the placement.

item.title: Claim: video shows acrobats building a towering, wave-like human pyramid in seconds
item.description: Clips watermarked “Grandora Show” or “Dola AI,” showing purple-clad performers stacking into swaying towers and “skyscrapers” in seconds, are circulating as real feats. Verdict: False. Fact-checkers at Lead Stories and BOOM found the videos are AI-generated, pointing to tell-tale errors such as blurred or missing faces, malformed hands and people appearing mid-tower. Lead Stories notes that building a real record-setting human tower took more than three minutes. Real human towers do exist, such as Catalonia’s castells, but they’re built slowly and carefully; the viral clips aren’t footage of any real event. Why it matters: It’s a reminder that “impossible” stunt clips are increasingly synthetic; look for watermarks and AI-content labels before sharing.

item.title: The first working nuclear clocks: teams in Vienna and Beijing keep time with thorium-229 nuclei
item.description: Two papers published in Nature this week report the first nuclear clocks, which keep time using a transition inside the atomic nucleus of thorium-229 rather than electrons, as atomic clocks do. A team at TU Wien with Germany’s PTB built a clock that stabilizes itself: thorium in a crystal absorbs laser light only at exactly the right frequency, and the laser is automatically corrected. It ran for more than 24 hours without intervention, with precision of about 10−15 over a day, roughly one second in 30 million years. A separate team led by Tsinghua University reported a clock about six times as stable as Vienna’s and showed that two separately grown crystals kept the same time, a sign the clocks could be reproduced, the South China Morning Post reports. Writing in Nature, metrologist Akio Kawasaki called the results “a milestone in the field of metrology.” These are lab prototypes and are not yet as precise as the best optical atomic clocks; TU Wien says precision still has to be “drastically improved” with stronger lasers and better crystals. The Vienna team also used its clock in a dark-matter search and found no signal. Why it matters: Because nuclei are far less sensitive to outside disturbances, such clocks could eventually beat today’s best timekeepers, which underpin GPS, telecom networks and tests of fundamental physics.

item.title: OpenAI says Iranian and Russian operations used ChatGPT to get fake bylines and narratives into real news outlets
item.description: OpenAI said Thursday it banned accounts behind two influence operations. An Iran-origin network created seven fake journalist personas and used ChatGPT to pitch and polish articles, mainly about the U.S.–Iran war; OpenAI found almost 100 articles published or syndicated across about a dozen small-to-medium outlets. It said the activity looked like “a commercial actor running a for-hire influence campaign” but couldn’t identify who. A Russian network OpenAI calls “Dark Clark” ran a fake Latin American think tank with real employees who apparently didn’t know they were working for a Russian group, and used ChatGPT mostly to write reports to its bosses. OpenAI rated the two campaigns 4 and 5 on its six-point impact scale, the first time it has reported operations it considers high-impact. The attribution and impact ratings are OpenAI’s own and haven’t been independently verified; OpenAI does not name a government agency behind either campaign. Some outlets that ran the articles have since removed the author pages. Why it matters: It shows AI-assisted propaganda reaching readers through legitimate-looking outlets, not just bot accounts, which is exactly why this site checks every story against several independent sources.

item.title: Google launches “Gemini agent,” an AI co-worker for businesses with its own Workspace account
item.description: At a Google Cloud event Thursday, Google introduced a single Gemini agent that can be given “objectives, not just instructions,” in the words of Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian: it plans work, writes and runs code, and connects to company systems such as Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack and Jira. It gets its own Workspace identity and email address, and its actions leave an audit trail attributed to the agent. Users can pick models, starting with Anthropic’s Claude alongside Google’s own. CEO Sundar Pichai said Gemini has more than a billion monthly users. The agent launches first for business customers, with Google saying a consumer version will come later. Availability starts as a limited preview for select business customers, and capability claims are Google’s own until independent testing. Agents that can take actions raise new security and error risks, which is why Google is stressing audit trails and admin controls. Why it matters: Agents that act on their own, not just answer questions, are where workplace AI is heading, including for Alberta employers that use Google or Microsoft tools.

item.title: Jaryd's News — Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Environment Canada flags the season’s first accumulating snow for Alberta this Thanksgiving weekend, possibly including the Edmonton–Calgary corridor; Smith says she has already voted for Alberta to stay in Canada and urges Albertans to do the same; Edmonton Public Schools trustees order a review of enrolment policies that can keep children without immigration status out of class; Toronto-born poet Anne Carson wins the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature; Trump says Canada wants a trade deal but “we’re not satisfied,” repeating that he wants cars built in the U.S.; Russian strike on passenger buses in Kramatorsk kills at least 30; public transport halted in two Donetsk cities; Pentagon tells U.S. Central Command to be ready to resume major combat against Iran; Trump has not decided; Isaias becomes the Atlantic’s first hurricane of the season, with landfall on the U.S. northern Gulf Coast expected late Friday or early Saturday; Margaret Hamilton, who led the software team that helped land Apollo 11 on the moon, has died at 90; Brent crude jumps above US$104 on Iran-strike reports; TSX futures hit a three-month low as bond yields climb; Ottawa is “considering the options” on the foreign homebuyer ban that expires Jan. 1, Champagne says. Plus Viral on social, Science corner, AI news and advances, Markets and the next Oilers game.

item.title: Environment Canada flags the season’s first accumulating snow for Alberta this Thanksgiving weekend, possibly including the Edmonton–Calgary corridor
item.description: Environment and Climate Change Canada issued a special weather statement at 4:43 a.m. MDT Thursday covering the City of Edmonton, St. Albert and Sherwood Park, among other regions. It says rain will spread across northern Alberta today, change to snow on Friday in west-central regions and over much of the province by Saturday, then taper off from north to south on Sunday. Many areas are expected to see accumulating snow on Saturday, “possibly including the Calgary-Edmonton corridor.” The heaviest amounts are expected in the west, including Grande Cache, Hinton and Jasper National Park, where totals could exceed 20 cm; amounts elsewhere remain uncertain. Edmonton’s forecast calls for 5 to 10 mm of rain tonight, rain Friday with temperatures steady near 7°C, rain or snow Saturday with a high of 2°C, then a sunny Thanksgiving Monday with a high of 8°C. A special weather statement is Environment Canada’s lowest-level alert; it is not a snowfall warning. The agency itself says amounts outside the western mountains and foothills are uncertain, so expect the forecast to change; check Environment Canada and 511 Alberta before driving. Why it matters: It’s a long weekend with heavy highway travel; the agency warns of “quickly changing and deteriorating travel conditions,” especially on routes west toward Hinton and Jasper.

item.title: Smith says she has already voted for Alberta to stay in Canada and urges Albertans to do the same
item.description: Speaking to the Leduc, Nisku and Wetaskiwin Chamber of Commerce on Wednesday afternoon, Premier Danielle Smith said she has already cast her ballot for option one on the sovereignty question — Alberta remaining in Canada — “and I hope to be able to convince all of you to vote the same way.” She urged a yes vote on the referendum’s other nine questions. Smith said she understands lingering resentment toward former prime minister Justin Trudeau but argued Ottawa’s approach has changed under Prime Minister Mark Carney, pointing to pipeline approvals and the Canada–Alberta energy agreement. “I am going to do whatever I can to convince as many Albertans as possible that Canada can work,” she said. Smith is backing “remain” on separation but “yes” on the other nine questions, which deal with immigration and the Constitution, so her position is not a blanket endorsement of the status quo. Her comments on Ottawa reflect her own assessment; they came the same day Ottawa highlighted about $8 billion in Alberta defence spending (see Oct. 7 archive). Why it matters: The premier is now openly campaigning for “remain” 11 days before the Oct. 19 vote, which asks whether to start the process toward a binding separation referendum.

item.title: Edmonton Public Schools trustees order a review of enrolment policies that can keep children without immigration status out of class
item.description: Edmonton Public School Board trustees passed a motion at their Oct. 6 meeting directing the board’s Policy Review Committee to review its policies and recommend changes to align them with “every child’s right to education” as described in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. The motion, brought by trustee Sarah Doll, says current registration and enrolment rules “may create a barrier” for children who aren’t eligible for provincial funding because of their immigration status. The review is to be informed by the administration’s advice on operational, legal and financial considerations. Under Alberta’s Education Act, boards may charge a fee to students who don’t meet resident-student eligibility. This starts a policy review; it does not change who can enrol today. Recommendations would come back to trustees for a decision, and eligibility for provincial education funding is set by the province, not the board. Why it matters: Alberta’s largest school division is acting less than two weeks before a referendum that includes questions on immigrants’ access to social services, Global News noted.

item.title: Toronto-born poet Anne Carson wins the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
item.description: The Swedish Academy awarded the prize Thursday to Anne Carson, 76, “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.” The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, about $1.7 million. Permanent secretary Ingrid Carlberg said Carson took the call in Iceland, where she was “listening to the wind.” A poet, essayist, translator and classics scholar, Carson is known for books that mix poetry, essay and fiction, including Autobiography of Red, Nox and Eros the Bittersweet, and for translations of Sappho, Sophocles and Euripides. She earned three degrees at the University of Toronto, whose president, Melanie Woodin, called it “a very proud moment.” The Globe and Mail counts her as the third Canadian to win the literature Nobel. Carson has lived in Iceland, where she and her husband were granted citizenship in 2022, AP reports; she remains a Canadian author. The Nobel honours a body of work, not a single book. The dollar figure is an approximate conversion of the prize money. Why it matters: It’s the first literature Nobel for a Canadian since Alice Munro in 2013, and a spotlight on Canadian writing heading into Thanksgiving weekend.

item.title: Trump says Canada wants a trade deal but “we’re not satisfied,” repeating that he wants cars built in the U.S.
item.description: Asked at the White House on Wednesday about Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers, whose new ad calls to “end this tariff war” with Canada, President Donald Trump said: “Canada has been very difficult to deal with … Canada would like to make a deal, but we’re not satisfied with them.” Trump repeated claims that Canada has charged tariffs of up to 400 per cent on U.S. dairy and that the U.S. is “losing $90 billion a year” trading with Canada, and said, “We want to make our own cars. We don’t want them to make cars for us.” He said he took Rogers’ ad as a call for Canada to make a deal rather than criticism of his approach. The 400 per cent and $90 billion figures are Trump’s own and weren’t sourced. Canada’s steep dairy tariffs apply only to imports above duty-free quotas negotiated under CUSMA, and trade-balance figures vary depending on whether energy and services are counted. Why it matters: It signals no quick end to the Canada–U.S. tariff dispute that has continued since talks broke down in August, which matters for Alberta exporters and jobs.

item.title: Russian strike on passenger buses in Kramatorsk kills at least 30; public transport halted in two Donetsk cities
item.description: A Russian strike hit passenger buses in Kramatorsk, in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, on Thursday morning. The city council said at least 30 people were killed and 18 injured; Ukraine’s emergency service later put the toll at 33, the Kyiv Independent reported. Officials said a glide bomb was used, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of dead could still rise. Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians and ordered public transport suspended in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk. Overnight, Ukraine’s air force said it intercepted or suppressed 126 of 142 drones, and a jet-powered drone damaged an apartment building in Kyiv, where power outages worsened. Tolls differ by agency and were rising through the morning: the city council said 30, the State Emergency Service 33. Casualty figures come from Ukrainian officials; Russia had not commented on the Kramatorsk strike in these reports. Why it matters: Halting buses in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, the main Ukrainian-held cities in Donetsk, cuts daily services for civilians near the front as Russia steps up attacks before winter.

item.title: Pentagon tells U.S. Central Command to be ready to resume major combat against Iran; Trump has not decided
item.description: The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command several days ago to finish preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran, U.S. officials told Axios. NBC News reported that Trump and his national security team have discussed possibly resuming large-scale operations in the coming weeks, including before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The Atlantic first reported that the White House had asked for strike options. Sources told Axios that any renewed campaign would be expected to include heavy bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets. No date has been set, and people familiar with the talks told NBC no decision has been made. All three reports rely on unnamed officials, and planning is not a decision to strike; militaries routinely prepare options. The war has been in an uneasy stalemate for about three months, with smaller Iranian attacks on shipping cutting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Why it matters: Oil jumped more than 4 per cent on the reports (see Business), which feeds straight into Canadian gas prices and Alberta’s royalty revenue.

item.title: Isaias becomes the Atlantic’s first hurricane of the season, with landfall on the U.S. northern Gulf Coast expected late Friday or early Saturday
item.description: At 7 a.m. CDT (6 a.m. MDT) the U.S. National Hurricane Center put Hurricane Isaias about 620 km south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River with maximum sustained winds of 130 km/h, moving east-northeast at 15 km/h. It is forecast to strengthen through early Friday and remain a strong hurricane as it nears the coast Friday night. A hurricane warning runs from Ocean Springs, Miss., to the Bay/Gulf County line in the Florida Panhandle, and a storm-surge warning from the mouth of the Mississippi to the Steinhatchee River, Fla., with surge of 1.5 to 2 metres possible in parts of Alabama and Mississippi. Florida’s Okaloosa County ordered mandatory evacuations of coastal zones, Gulf Shores and Orange Beach, Ala., urged visitors to leave, and some Gulf oil wells paused production, AP reported. AP notes Isaias formed one day short of tying a 1905 record for the latest first Atlantic hurricane of a season, which has been unusually quiet because of a strong El Niño. The exact landfall point and peak strength can still shift; rely on NHC advisories over social-media model screenshots. Why it matters: Canadians with Thanksgiving-weekend trips to the Gulf Coast or the U.S. Southeast should expect disruptions and follow local evacuation orders.

item.title: Margaret Hamilton, who led the software team that helped land Apollo 11 on the moon, has died at 90
item.description: MIT said Margaret Hamilton died Sept. 30. Hired in 1965 as the first programmer on the Apollo project at MIT’s Instrumentation Lab, she went on to lead the team writing the on-board flight software for the crewed missions; by 1968 more than 400 people were working on Apollo’s software. During Apollo 11’s descent in 1969, computer alarms warned that the guidance computer was overloaded. Because the software was designed to drop lower-priority tasks and keep the most important ones running, the landing could continue rather than be aborted, CBS Boston and MIT report. NASA credits Hamilton with popularizing the concept of “software engineering,” and she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. Apollo’s software was a team effort involving hundreds of people at MIT and NASA; Hamilton led the on-board flight software group. MIT says a memorial service is planned for the spring in Cambridge, Mass. Why it matters: The error-handling ideas her team built for Apollo underpin the safety-critical software used today in aircraft, medical devices and spacecraft.

item.title: Brent crude jumps above US$104 on Iran-strike reports; TSX futures hit a three-month low as bond yields climb
item.description: Oil surged Thursday morning after reports that the U.S. is preparing options to resume strikes on Iran. Yahoo Finance data showed Brent crude futures at US$104.49 a barrel at 7:05 a.m. MDT, up 4.3 per cent, and U.S. crude at US$92.22, up 4.5 per cent; NBC News said Brent briefly topped US$105. The Globe and Mail cited Iranian attacks on shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz and output cuts in the U.S. Gulf ahead of Hurricane Isaias. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 5.32 per cent. S&P 500 futures were down about 0.4 per cent and Nasdaq 100 futures about 0.6 per cent, and Reuters reported TSX futures were down about 0.5 per cent after briefly touching their lowest level since early July, a day after the TSX’s steepest drop in four months.
